ROSEMONT, Ill. — A new outlet mall under construction here — the first enclosed mall to be built in the Chicago area in over a decade — is both a departure for the outlet industry and a major new attraction for this close-in Chicago suburb long known as a convention and business hub.
An interior shot of "Fashion Outlets of Chicago," undergoing contruction, in Rosemont, IL.
The $250 million mall, Fashion Outlets of Chicago, is scheduled to open this summer. The two-level, 530,000-square-foot center is being co-developed by AWE Talisman, aFlorida-based company that also owns outlet centers in Las Vegas and Santa Fe, N.M., and the Macerich Company of Santa Monica, Calif.
“The project is a game changer on several levels,” said Arthur Weiner, chairman of AWE Talisman. “We’re in a prized area with a higher level of construction and amenities than you would normally see at an outlet center. We also have a pretty good store list.”
The mall, which is 90 percent leased, is focused on luxury retailers like Saks Fifth Avenue’s Off 5th, Last Call by Neiman Marcus, Bloomingdale’s the Outlet Store and Barneys New York.
In addition, there are outlets by top fashion names like Prada, Gucci, Giorgio Armani, Tory Burch and Michael Kors.
The developer and the retailers hope to shake up Chicago’s retail scene with the new mall.
To date, outlet stores have not been very prominent in the Chicago area, with the nearest outlet center — Chicago Premium Outlets in Aurora, Ill. — about 40 miles from downtown Chicago. But Rosemont is a closer suburb and only 20 minutes from Chicago’s Michigan Avenue, where all of the above stores have thriving full-price locations.
Arnie Orlick, senior vice president of outlets for Bloomingdale’s, said that the mall’s focus on luxury — one of the fastest-growing segments of the outlet market — bodes well for the project.
“When all of these retailers go into a mall,” he said, “you know they’re going to attract many more customers than a traditional outlet center.”
Neil Stern, senior partner with McMillanDoolittle, a Chicago-based retail consulting firm, said that the mall reflected a shift in the outlet business. “There used to be a clear divide between outlets and regular retail, but that doesn’t really exist anymore,” he said. “Today we’re seeing outlets that are almost the equivalent of full-line stores.”
Specifically, outlets used to be places where retailers and manufacturers disposed of closeout and past-season goods. Today, however, they tend to be separate divisions within their companies and tend to have their own supply chains and customer bases.
“It’s the same brands and labels but they’ve engineered the process to get the price points more in line with the outlet environment,” said Mr. Stern.
Robert Wallstrom, president of Saks’s Off 5th outlet division, said that Off 5th was merchandised for a different customer than Saks’s regular stores.
“There’s some crossover between the full-price and off-price customers, but it’s only about 10 percent,” he said. “What we’re trying to create is a luxury value department store.”
The location is also a departure. In the past, outlet centers were often bare-bones affairs located far from major population centers. Fashion Outlets, however, is a quick drive from downtown Chicago.
“We’re excited about it,” said Wayne A. Hussey, senior vice president of properties and store development at Neiman Marcus. “Rosemont is an amazing area in terms of the critical mass of hotels and restaurants and it’s very close to the airport as well.”
That last comment is something of an understatement. Rosemont is not just close to O’Hare International Airport. It’s literally next door.
This proximity was one of the main drivers of the project, according to Mr. Weiner, of AWE Talisman. “Outlet shopping is fueled by tourism,” he said. “Visitors can be 50 percent or more of the business.”

Every other year, the Festival des Arts Visuels, which is devoted to photography and held in Vevey, Switzerland, selects an artist to receive $42,000 to fund a new project. As a member of the festival’s jury last week, I helped review the work of 750 photographers from 63 countries. The winner was Augustin Rebetez, a young Swiss whose photos, videos and drawings can be frightening yet weirdly playful and touching. Awkward home scenes, with walls that come to life and beds that breathe, are filled with demented twists and creepy characters. The fairytale world of his videos is as unsettling as the early work of David Lynch and the claymation art of Nathalie Djurberg — but also tender in the way that Tim Burton’s work can be.
Rebetez likes to work in Norway in the winter because of the long, dark days there. The video “The Dinner of the Lonely Man” was made in an empty house in the country’s north that he has returned to several times over the years. He had been told that the owner of the house, whom he never met but who can be seen in the video’s painting, lived by himself and was very lonely. That loneliness inspired the video’s love story.
This morning I spoke with Rebetez about his work over the phone — he was in Lagos, Nigeria, to premiere a film, “Cowboy Noir,” that he shot with collective he belongs to. “I always work at night,” he told me. “I never take pictures during the day. If I have to work during the day, I will close the curtains and make it black. If you go to the theater, it won’t be a white cube like in a gallery. It will be a black cube. Night has a power. I often use a flashlight. I always use my light.”
Rebetez often works in abandoned spaces that happen to be rich with objects he can use in his videos and photographs. The phones below, for example, came from an old cupboard in an abandoned graphite mine in Norway. “They were like a treasure for me,” he said, “these old phones, not able to communicate anymore.” So he tried to make something “like a labyrinth, like a maze” out of them.
Augustin Rebetez
This picture is an example of Rebetez’s recurring interest in dreams and home.
Augustin Rebetez
And these roller skates show how the objects in his photos often take on human characteristics.
Augustin Rebetez
“I am not able to take something as it exists,” Rebetez said of his work. “I have to find a way to change something. When I draw people I do them with three hands or with the leg behind the head.” That’s why he plans to use his grant money to photograph circus performers. “I would like to bring acrobats into my work because they are people who can do things with their bodies that other people can’t. Re “The Texas Abortion Experiment” (column, July 21):
Ross Douthat’s analysis of the means by which Irish women obtain abortions does not represent the realities of their situation. In addition to the considerable struggles of meeting the cost of travel, accommodation and time off from work, there is no guarantee that passage abroad will be unimpeded by the state, a partner or even the medical profession.
Numerous cases exist in which Irish women were prevented from leaving the country and forced to endure legal proceedings, prolonging psychological distress and seriously compromising medical safety by delaying care. The issue is not whether these cases occur in large numbers, but that they occur at all.
The new Texas legislation will deplete abortion clinics to the point where most women will have no option but to leave the state to get care. If Ireland is the best example of what we can expect to see happen in Texas, the future is bleak.

The writer, a doctor from Northern Ireland, is a Ph.D. candidate in reproductive health and demography at the University of Texas at Austin.
Ross Douthat ignores the reality facing Texas women. Studies show that the best way to reduce unintended pregnancy and the need for abortion is through access to information and affordable birth control, which is what many of the European countries highlighted by Mr. Douthat offer their citizens.
Gov. Rick Perry has done the opposite at every turn, opposing sex education programs and restricting women’s access to birth control and other basic care. Texas has the highest rate of uninsured women in the country, and to compound that, Mr. Perry and his allies slashed the budget for women’s health, closing more than 60 health centers.
In the Rio Grande Valley, Planned Parenthood was forced to close centers that provided preventive care like birth control and cancer screenings to women in the poorest areas of the state.
Dozens more health centers will likely close because of the bill signed by Governor Perry last week, leaving women in rural areas with nowhere to go for a safe, legal abortion. The alarming reality is that years of bad public policy mean that most will be left with no real options for getting the health care they need.
CECILE RICHARDSPresident, Planned ParenthoodFederation of AmericaNew York, July 23, 2013
Ross Douthat asks, “What happens to a modern society when abortion is restricted?” Examining the case of Ireland, he concludes that abortion restrictions have not harmed Irish women. I suggest that he look at the experience of women in pre-Roe v. Wade America. Women had illegal abortions and were injured as a result.
After my illegal abortion, in 1965, I was hospitalized with an infection because nonsterile instruments had been used. I know other women whose illegal abortions resulted in hemorrhages. We wouldn’t have chosen to have abortions, but unwanted pregnancies occur.
Reliable numbers in Ireland are probably hard to come by, since most women wouldn’t wish to publicize their abortions. But undoubtedly some brave Irish women might talk to Mr. Douthat. He would learn what happens when women have no recourse to abortion services that are local, legal and safe.
Ross Douthat’s column includes some important facts. He says Ireland’s “maternal health outcomes have long looked much better than those of its neighbors ... maternal mortality still placed the country well within the European norm.”
Ireland’s restrictions on abortion have long been known if not applauded, so the consequence of better or at least status quo maternal health rates should not be surprising.
We should take a lesson. The country, by and large predominantly Catholic, has a history of traditional values where each life is respected and has inviolable rights. We should look to our Constitution and see how similar these ideas were at the time it was written.
Let’s take a history lesson and learn from our own beginnings as well as from a country like Ireland.

STOCKHOLM – Ending the so-called home ice curse, Sweden defeated Switzerland, 5-1, to win the gold medal at the International Ice Hockey Federation world championships on Sunday. Earlier, Alex Galchenyuk scored twice in the shootout to give the United States a 3-2 win over Finland in the bronze medal game.
Before Sweden’s triumph, no host team had won the world championships since the Soviet Union in 1986. The victory moves the Swedes into the No. 1 position in the I.I.H.F. World Ranking. It is Sweden’s first world title since 2006.
Henrik Sedin, the 2010 N.H.L. scoring champion from the Vancouver Canucks, led the way with two goals and an assist in front of a sell-out crowd of 12,500 at the Globen Arena.
“It feels great,” Sedin said. “To play in front of your home fans in your country and to be able to win, it doesn’t happen often. That’s pretty amazing.”
With its second-place finish, Switzerland remarkably earned its first medal since capturing bronze in 1953. The Swiss previously won silver in 1935.
It is virtually unheard-of for a medal in senior men’s I.I.H.F. competition to go to a team outside the “Big Seven” hockey countries: Canada, the Czech Republic, Finland, Russia, Slovakia, Sweden, and the United States.
The last time it happened at the world championships was when Switzerland won its previous medal. At the Olympics, West Germany provided a rare exception to the rule when it captured the bronze medal at the 1976 Winter Games in Innsbruck, Austria.
The Swiss won nine straight games before losing to Sweden in the final.
Switzerland opened the scoring at 4 minutes 45 seconds. Defenseman Roman Josi, who plays for the N.H.L.’s Nashville Predators and was named the tournament’s most valuable player, cut hard to the net and put a backhander through the five hole of Swedish goalie Jhonas Enroth of the Buffalo Sabres. Enroth claimed best goalie honors at the tournament.
Less than three minutes later, Sweden made it 1-1 when Erik Gustafsson of the Philadelphia Flyers scooped up the rebound from a Fredrik Pettersson shot and put it past Swiss netminder Martin Gerber’s outstretched left pad.
Halfway through the period, Sweden got the game’s first power play when Andres Ambuhl was penalized for checking to the head of Loui Eriksson of the Dallas Stars. Eriksson’s linemates, the Sedin twins, teamed up to give Sweden a 2-1 lead at 11:42. Henrik converted a nice cross-ice pass from his brother Daniel into a gaping net, putting the puck off a Swiss defender.
Sweden’s Gabriel Landeskog, the captain of the Colorado Avalanche, capitalized on a Julian Vauclair giveaway at the Swiss blue line. Landeskog fired a shot at Gerber, and Simon Hjalmarsson pushed the rebound into the net to make it 3-1 Sweden at 7:15 of the third period.
Henrik Sedin’s slapper from the right point went off Eriksson’s leg and in with 4:23 left, giving the Swedes a 4-1 lead. The play was video-reviewed before the goal was ruled good. The partisan crowd, full of yellow jerseys, exploded with jubilation, clapping rhythmically.
Henrik Sedin added a short-handed empty-net goal to clinch the victory with 3:24 remaining. The Swedes exchanged their regular helmets for golden ones before leaping on to the ice to celebrate at the final buzzer.
“We’ve been to the Stanley Cup finals before,” said Daniel Sedin, recalling Vancouver’s 2011 battle with the Boston Bruins. “We lost in the seventh game, and that’s obviously tough. We won Olympic gold [in 2006], and this has got to be up there with Olympic gold, I’d say.
In the bronze medal game, United States captain Paul Stastny, from the Colorado Avalanche, and Craig Smith of the Nashville Predators each had a goal and an assist against Finland in the first period.
Stastny tied Russia’s Ilya Kovalchuk for second place in the tournament points derby (15), one behind Finland’s Petri Kontiola, who was named best forward for 2013.
Lauri Korpikoski of the Phoenix Coyotes scored twice for the Finns in the last 10 minutes of the third period to tie the game and send it to overtime.
The bronze was the first medal for the United States since a squad coached by Peter Laviolette (currently with the Philadelphia Flyers) captured bronze in 2004 in the Czech Republic.
“It’s great for our country to get a medal here,” said forward T.J. Oshie of the St. Louis Blues. “Hopefully it’ll draw a little more attention for the U.S. in this tournament.”
This was also a fine showing for teenage American talent. As the shootout hero, Galchenyuk, 19, built on his success at the 2013 under-20 world championships in Ufa, Russia, where he helped the United States win gold.
Under the playoff format adopted by the I.I.H.F in 1992, John Gibson, 19, became the youngest goalie ever to win a medal for the United States.
Gibson, the starting goalie for the Ontario Hockey League’s Kitchener Rangers, took best goalie and tournament most valuable player honors at the 2013 under-20 world championships.
These were the last world championships before the 2014 Olympics in Sochi, Russia. The next tournament will take place in Belarus from May 9 to 25, 2014.

âWe are about the fillies: they provide consistency over generations,â Dinny Phipps said.
The goal has always been to make money, and to do so, the family operates with the same discipline it employs at Bessemer Trust, a company established with the familyâs original United States Steel fortune that now manages more than $88 billion for some of the worldâs wealthiest people. This talent and the exacting standards have been passed from generation to generation. Artwork by the Canadian artist Rodney Graham at 303 Gallery’s new Chelsea location.
New York City art galleries tend to move around a lot. But even by those standards, the iconic
303 Gallery
has been unusually itinerant. Since it was founded in 1984 at 303 Park Avenue South by its director Lisa Spellman, it has had homes in the East Village and SoHo, and at two addresses in Chelsea. Today, it throws open its brand-new industrial doors at a third Chelsea location, a bilevel space on West 24th Street tucked below the High Line. Designed by the architecture firm
StudioMDA
for 303, it’s an airy, light-filled space that doubles the gallery’s square footage, with skylights, glass floors and the columns of the High Line running through, all protected by a cast concrete facade.
Graham’s “Cactus Fan,” 2013.
Spellman has a well-earned reputation for cultivating the careers of mega-watt stars, including Robert Gober, Stephen Shore, Karen Kilimnik, Mary Heilman and Doug Aitken (whose most recent piece for the gallery centered on the demolition of its old 21st Street space), and the new location will offer her more resources to do that. The inaugural exhibition is by the Canadian artist Rodney Graham, whose new work features more conceptually driven photography with wide-ranging visual inspirations, from the work of 19th-century artists like Thomas Eakins and Carl Spitzweg to Abstract Expressionism and Color Field painting. It’s only fitting that Graham’s show should kick off the new space, according to Spellman, since she’s worked with him for nearly 20 years. “He is such an important artist, but important to me as well,” she says. Of course, she could say the same about most of the names on her roster. “I try to work with artists I feel a connection to,” she adds, “since that helps determine the quality and longevity of the relationship.” Maybe that support is why so many of them show at MoMA, LACMA and the Venice Biennale, though Spellman refuses to take credit. “I think they just make good works because they are good artists!”
She’s not as loyal when it comes to spaces, however. 303 will remain in its new digs for just two years before moving yet again. Next, it will return to its old block on 21st Street, where it will occupy the first two floors of a residential development scheduled to open in 2015.

When the stage director Doug Fitch and the filmmaker Edouard Getaz speak about their collaborations, they inevitably touch on matters of scale — ways of making tiny objects seem huge, and sometimes the opposite.

Manipulating perceptions of scale has become their trademark, most notably in productions for the New York Philharmonic — two operas,Ligeti’s “Grande Macabre”and Janacek’s “Cunning Little Vixen,” and a ballet project,“A Dancer’s Dream,”based on a pair of Stravinsky works. Scenes enacted in a puppet theater on the stage are also projected onto large screens in those works, and that fascination explains the name of their production company,Giants Are Small.
Mr. Fitchand Mr. Getaz (pronounced JEH-tah) are now expanding in other directions. “A Dancer’s Dream” will be shown in high-definition in movie theaters, starting next Thursday. And they are working on an iPad app, built around their 2008 Los Angeles Philharmonic production of Prokofiev’s “Peter and the Wolf.”
What has also kept their Midtown Manhattan offices and their Brooklyn studio buzzing in recent weeks is “Hot Culture,” a Web series starring Wigglesworth, a puppet who, posing as an arts journalist (“Hot Culture” is the name of his TV chat show), bluffs his way backstage at cultural events and inadvertently provides insights into an artist’s work. The episodes last only two minutes, and in the first, to be posted on Giants Are Small’sYouTubechannel on Thursday, Wigglesworth focuses on Mercedes-Benz Fashion Weekby interviewingthe designer Isaac Mizrahi.
The episodes are “fairly low-budget things — we don’t want to overproduce them,” Mr. Fitch said. “That’s part of the charm and fun of it. They are clearly done guerrilla style.”
Mr. Getaz, who oversees the practical aspects of the team’s work, defined low budget as roughly $5,000 an episode.
They work close to deadline. The day before the first episode was taped, Mr. Fitch and his puppet — a big-headed, bespectacled character, balding but with a halo of unruly brown hair and a black mustache, who Mr. Fitch began creating when he was 10 — presided over a table reading of the six-page script. Plot points were still being actively debated. Mr. Mizrahi’s part was to be mostly ad-libbed.
The team also batted around preliminary ideas for the second episode. The subject will be the New York City Opera’sproduction of “Anna Nicole,”Mark-Anthony Turnage’s opera about the sex symbol Anna Nicole Smith, and the episode will go online in mid-September. There will be six episodes before Christmas, Mr. Getaz said, but he and Mr. Fitch said that they were not sure what the remaining four would be about, except that the Park Avenue Armory would figure in one of them.
“It’s an old fantasy that Doug and I have entertained for quite a few years,” Mr. Getaz said: “to have a puppet which would be present on the Web on a regular basis. And it just evolved organically.”
What it evolved from was “The Unspoken Side of Show Business,” a series Giants Are Small created to help the New York Philharmonic promote “A Dancer’s Dream.” In that series, which is more humorous than overtly promotional, Wigglesworth posed as a casting director who promised to find a bankable star to play the opera’s magician.
Sara Mearns,the dancer who starred in “Dream,” appeared in the series. So did Alan Gilbert, the Philharmonic’s conductor and music director. In the final episode, shown shortly after Mr. Gilberthalted a concertbecause of a ringing cellphone in the audience, Wigglesworth telephones the conductor during a concert. Mr. Gilbert continues conducting as he takes the call.
“I just think they’ve got the perfect combination of real sensitivity and irreverence, which is just what the New York Philharmonic needs,” Mr. Gilbert said, referring not only to the Wigglesworth production — which he said he enjoyed making — but also to Giants Are Small’s production style.
Mr. Gilbert has been one of the company’s strongest champions. His relationship with Mr. Fitch goes back to his years at Harvard, in the 1980s, when Mr. Fitch was the drama tutor at the Adams House student residence, where Mr. Gilbert lived. (Wigglesworth also has a Harvard connection: Mr. Fitch brought the puppet to his admissions interview — he insists the puppet helped get him accepted — and took the name Wigglesworth from his dormitory.)
In the late 1990s, when Mr. Fitch was working mainly as an interior designer, Mr. Gilbert engaged him to do his New York apartment — as didthe violinist Joshua Bell.And when Mr. Fitch began directing opera, Mr. Gilbert began hiring him to oversee productions in Santa Fe, N.M., and later brought him to the Philharmonic for its staged concerts.
Mr. Fitch, 54, teamed up with Mr. Getaz, 40, in 2005, to work on a version of Stravinsky’s “Histoire du Soldat.” They also worked on “Freud’s Magic Power,” a 2008 film by Mr. Getaz, before becoming Giants Are Small, for which they also took on a third, mostly silent partner, Frédéric Gumy, whose role is to find investors and underwriters. Investors may not make anything back on projects like “Hot Culture,” but could see returns from “Peter and the Wolf in Hollywood,” an iPad app in the works.
That project, based on a reconfiguration of the “Peter and the Wolf” story that Giants Are Small built for the Los Angeles Philharmonic in 2008, includes a prequel: Peter, a young Russian boy, flies to Los Angeles to be with his grandfather, a Russian immigrant turned hippie who is partial to Russian surf music. They hear a news report with a warning that a wolf has escaped from the Los Angeles Zoo, and the rest is history, conveyed in its stage version by a performance of the Prokofiev score, and in the app by a reworked, interactive version of their stage production.
A reconfigured live staging of “Peter” is on the Giants Are Small drawing board as well, as are future iterations of “A Dancer’s Dream.” And Mr. Fitch and Mr. Getaz say they will spend much of the fall working on aproduction of H. K. Gruber’s “Gloria: A Pig Tale,”part of the New York Philharmonic Biennial of new music, with Mr. Gilbert conducting the Axiom Ensemble and singers from the Juilliard School, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art on May 29.
“It’s so easy at the Philharmonic, with its great capacity, for things to look totally worked out, with an impersonal tinge,” Mr. Gilbert said. “And the reason I’ve enjoyed working with Doug is that he lets the work process show through. It’s very much the fingerprint of the potter on the side of the pot — the idea that not everything has to look totally glossy.”

Brad DeLong
has the best piece I’ve seen on Bernanke rage among the hedge funders. His point is that the hedgies keep thinking of the Fed as if it were a rogue trader driving prices away from their natural value, like JP Morgan’s London Whale, rather than as a central bank trying to achieve full employment and target inflation. Hence their rage at the failure of bond prices to collapse the way they “should”.
I’d riff on this a bit further. Jerry DeWitt, a former Pentecostal preacher, led a secular service Sunday in Baton Rouge, La. Many atheists miss a sense of belonging, he said.
BATON ROUGE, La. — It would have been easy to mistake what was happening in a hotel ballroom here for a religious service. All the things that might be associated with one were present Sunday: 80 people drawn by a common conviction. Exhortations to service. Singing and light swaying. An impassioned sermon.

Billed as Louisiana’s first atheist service and titled “Joie de Vivre: To Delight in Being Alive,” it was presided over by Jerry DeWitt, a small, charismatic man dressed all in black with slick, shiny hair.
“Oh, it’s going to be so hard to not say, ‘Can I get an amen?’ ” he said with a smile, warning people that this was going to be more like church than they might expect. “I want you to feel comfortable singing. And I want you to feel comfortable clapping your hands. I’m going to ask you to silence your cellphones, but I’m not going to ask you to turn them off. Because I want you to post.”
As Mr. DeWitt paced back and forth, speaking with a thick Southern accent, his breathy yet powerful voice occasionally cracked with emotion. The term may be a contradiction, but he is impossible to describe as anything but an atheist preacher.
Mr. DeWitt acts so much like a clergyman because he was one.
He was raised Pentecostal in DeRidder, La., a small town near the Texas border. In 2011, after 25 years as a preacher, he realized he had lost all connection to the religious point of view that had defined most of his life. He left the church and found himself ostracized in his hometown and from his family. Since then, Mr. DeWitt, 43, has become a prominent advocate of atheism, giving lectures around the region and providing an emotional counterpoint to more academic atheist exponents like Richard Dawkins and Christopher Hitchens.
With Sunday’s service — marking the start of Community Mission Chapel in Lake Charles, which Mr. DeWitt called a full-fledged atheist “church” — he wanted to bring some of the things that he had learned from his years as a religious leader to atheists in southern Louisiana.
The percentage of religiously unaffiliated Americans appears to be on the rise. A2012 Pew Research Center studyfound that while only about 6 percent identified as atheist or agnostic, they were among nearly 20 percent classified as religiously unaffiliated. That was up from 15 percent in 2007, a greater increase than for any traditional faith.
Mr. DeWitt counts himself among the hard-line atheists, but he believes that something may be lost when someone leaves the church — not just the parts about God, but also a sense of community and a connection to emotion.
“There are many people that even though they come to this realization, they miss the way the church works in a way that very few other communities can duplicate,” he said in a phone interview. “The secular can learn that just because we value critical thinking and the scientific method, that doesn’t mean we suddenly become disembodied and we can no longer benefit from our emotional lives.”
Some in the audience had a difficult time coming to atheism. Joshua Hammers, a member of an atheist organization in Lake Charles, said he had been completely separated from his community and social life when he left the Pentecostal church in which he was raised. For him, there was something comfortable, a reminder of childhood, about hearing Mr. DeWitt preach.
“We were at the Reason on the Bayou conference, and everything else was just like a lecture,” Mr. Hammers said, referring to a secular rally held in April at Louisiana State University. “Then Jerry got up, and he was just, you know, preaching the message. Most other atheist leaders are academics and intellectuals, and Jerry’s not like that. He’s just talking to your heart.”
Services are gaining traction as outlets for organized atheism in places like London, Houston, Sacramento and New York, as well as at universities with humanist chaplains. In a deeply conservative region like the Deep South, they can serve a vital purpose: providing a sense of camaraderie in what many have found to be a hostile environment for nonreligious people.
“Here, we have a very strong sense of community,” said Russell Rush, a former youth pastor from DeRidder. “When you go into an actual church, it’s almost like having a family reunion. When you leave that lifestyle, and leave that church life behind, a lot of times you can feel ostracized. Things like this let fellow atheists and agnostics know that they’re not alone.”
Mr. DeWitt sees services like his as giving a human shape to a broad intellectual movement that is in its infancy. He believes that he and the others in the room are building something meant to last.
“Though this movement has had starts and stops throughout world history, right now it’s important to remember thatwe are young,” he said after a singalong to a song of that name by the band Fun. “Someday, what you are doing will become normal. Isn’t that a feeling?”
Most of us need to be more active, but, Room for Debate asks, how do you know when that healthy habit has crossed the line?
Affirmative action hangs on, but the court has set a very high bar.
